b: For most people, Christmas trees have a relatively short lifespan once they’re harvested for sale. They spend a few weeks brightening up living rooms before being unceremoniously dragged to the curb or taken to a recycling center. But in Kentucky, those post-holiday evergreens have an entirely different destination: the bottom of a lake.

Through an initiative called “Christmas for the Fishes,” the Kentucky Department of Fish and Wildlife Resources (KDFWR) collects thousands of Christmas trees each year and sinks them into reservoirs throughout the state. What might otherwise become yard waste gets a second life as valuable fish habitat.

The program has been running since 2010, building on earlier habitat restoration efforts that date back to the 1980s. Today, Kentucky averages more than 5,000 donated trees annually, with more than 30 public drop-off locations commonly operating across the state.

And the results are encouraging. According to KDFWR Fish Habitat Biologist Spencer Phillips, previous electrofishing surveys have found a 500% increase in fish abundance at Christmas tree sites compared with areas without underwater structure.
Why Kentucky’s Lakes Need More Underwater Trees
Although Kentucky is known for its beautiful lakes, most of its larger bodies of water aren’t natural lakes. The state has more than 100 manmade lakes, with only three considered natural.

Many of these reservoirs were created by damming rivers and streams, leaving behind forests and other terrestrial habitat that initially became submerged. Those original trees provided excellent cover for fish, but they didn’t last forever.

As Phillips explains, many of Kentucky’s large reservoirs are now more than 60 years old. Over time, the original underwater forests have naturally decayed, leaving fish with fewer places to hide, feed, and reproduce. That’s where discarded Christmas trees come in.

Rather than allowing valuable habitat to disappear permanently, fisheries managers replenish it by sinking new evergreens into designated locations. The trees are secured with environmentally friendly weights and placed at varying depths, creating underwater brush piles that mimic some of the natural structure fish once relied upon.

These underwater structures provide several important benefits to local fish populations. Smaller fish can hide among the branches to escape larger predators, while algae and other organic material accumulate on the submerged wood, attracting aquatic insects and other small organisms that serve as food. Certain species also use the vegetation and woody structures as spawning habitat, while predatory fish such as largemouth bass take advantage of the branches for cover when ambushing prey.
In other words, these trees aren’t simply underwater hiding places: They become the foundation of miniature aquatic ecosystems that support fish throughout the food chain.
The Fish Benefiting From Kentucky’s Christmas Trees

For anglers, one of the most exciting aspects of the program is the variety of popular sportfish that associate with these submerged habitats. KDFWR specifically identifies largemouth bass, bluegill, and crappie as three species commonly found around Kentucky’s Christmas tree sites.

Largemouth bass are particularly well suited to this type of habitat. As ambush predators, they frequently position themselves around submerged branches, logs, and other structures, waiting for smaller fish to swim within striking distance. The cover also provides opportunities for bass to conserve energy while remaining close to potential prey.

Bluegill and crappie benefit in slightly different ways. As submerged trees begin to decay, their surfaces collect periphyton, a mixture of algae and other organisms. This attracts aquatic macroinvertebrates, creating additional feeding opportunities for smaller fish and eventually larger predators.

The result is a food web that develops around something as seemingly ordinary as a discarded Christmas tree. Phillips notes that the greatest concentrations of sportfish around these sites are often observed during fall and winter, when water temperatures are in the low 60s.
Wisconsin Researchers Found That Adding Trees Can Double Fish Production

Trees that have fallen into shallow water provide a refuge for fish, nutrients, and other benefits to lake ecosystems.
Photo credit: Wisconsin DNR.

Kentucky isn’t the only state discovering the benefits of underwater woody habitat. Research conducted by the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources at 92-acre Sanford Lake provides another compelling example of what happens when managers restore missing natural structure.

Researchers introduced 140 whole trees — primarily conifers along with some deciduous species — into the lake as part of a long-term investigation into whether adding woody habitat simply attracts existing fish or actually increases the lake’s ability to support more of them.
According to research team leader Greg Sass, the results showed that adding trees approximately doubled the amount of fish the lake could support.

Adding underwater cover can initially concentrate fish that were already living elsewhere in a lake. That can make a new brush pile appear productive without necessarily increasing the overall fish population.
However, the Wisconsin research found something more significant: The additional trees increased the lake’s fish production and carrying capacity.

Each submerged tree gradually became its own underwater community. Algae colonized the wood, aquatic invertebrates established themselves among the branches, and smaller fish moved in to find food and protection.

As leaves and wood decomposed, nutrients and energy moved through the aquatic food web, eventually supporting larger fish. Researchers also observed increases in largemouth bass and bluegill-pumpkinseed hybrids.

Still, anglers shouldn’t expect an immediate explosion of trophy-sized bass. Sass emphasizes that these ecological benefits take time to work their way through the food chain. Larger fish populations develop over longer periods, making sustained habitat restoration particularly important.

The research also offers some reassurance about environmental concerns. A 2024 analysis of the Sanford Lake project found no negative influence on water quality or clarity from the added trees. Together, the Kentucky and Wisconsin efforts demonstrate why natural structure is so important to healthy fisheries.
How Kentucky Residents Can Donate Their Christmas Trees
Kentucky residents who want to contribute to healthier fisheries can participate in the “Christmas for the Fishes” program after the holiday season. The process is simple:
Find a participating Christmas tree drop-off location through the KDFWR’s interactive map.
Remove all ornaments, tinsel, lights, and other decorations from the tree.
Bring the tree to an approved collection site during its designated collection period.
There is one particularly important requirement: Only real, live Christmas trees are accepted. Artificial trees cannot be used for the program.
Once collected, the trees are transported to designated reservoirs, weighted, and strategically submerged to create new fish habitat.

KDFWR uses electrofishing surveys and feedback from anglers to help determine where future habitat structures should be placed. This allows fisheries managers to evaluate existing sites and identify areas where additional cover could benefit local fish populations.
